q-92127.name: Question 1
q-92127.problem:
Which model represents the division problem below?

$$
2÷\frac{1}{8}=16
$$
q-92127.worked_solution:
To calculate $2÷\frac{1}{8}$, we need to divide each of $2$ wholes into $8$ equal parts, as shown below. This gives us the corresponding model for the given division problem.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14196242/assets/80d6548bd656ccfd0e4a2cd3dadd52671f7c9cfa648faf9ed293463adf3a92ba.png)

 

We get $2\times 8=16$ pieces in total.

q-92138.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14196242/assets/4af3047f22d112fd3b1c2689ffacc50a1ce3d53dc458327ba25038f448de9c61.png)

The model above represents $3$ wholes. Use this model to calculate the value of $3÷\frac{1}{7}.$
q-92138.worked_solution:
To calculate $3÷\frac{1}{7}$, we need to divide each of $3$ wholes into $7$ equal parts, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14196242/assets/19b5902c790191dff44c240bb518feeeea9f9ffe5c0c440ca94b59344b78e1eb.png)

 

We get $3\times 7=21$ pieces in total. 

Therefore:

$$
3÷\frac{1}{7}=21
$$

q-137761.name: Question 3
q-137761.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14196242/assets/675a66c94bee0deba216bf684aa2b74e6fa048ed62a3944dabe50cdbb88952f3.png)

Each of the six shapes in the model above represents one whole. From left to right, what numbers are missing from the division problem below?

$$
\boxed{\,\,}÷\frac{1}{3}=\boxed{\,\,}
$$
q-137761.worked_solution:
In the model, there are $6$ shapes. Each shape consists of $3$ pieces that each represent $\frac{1}{3}$ of a whole. There are $18$ pieces in total.

The model tells us that when we divide $6$ wholes into thirds, we will be left with $18$ pieces.

Hence, the division problem is:

$$
\boxed{\,6\,}÷\frac{1}{3}=\boxed{\,18\,}
$$

Therefore, the missing numbers are $6$ and $18.$
